Let me analyze this OIML certificate document.

Certificate details:
- Issuing Authority: Physikalisch-Technische Bundesanstalt (PTB), Germany
- Address: Bundesallee 100, 38116 Braunschweig
- Person responsible: Dr. O. Mack
- OIML Certificate No.: R76/2006-DE1-08.03, Revision 2
- Applicant: Sartorius Industrial Scales GmbH & Co. KG, Leinetal 2, 37120 Bovenden, Germany
- Manufacturer: same as applicant ("Manufacturer of the certified type is the applicant")
- Certified type: Nonautomatic electromechanical weighing instrument with or without lever system
- Types: BD SI 200, BG SI 200, DG SI 300, DX SI 300
- Recommendation: R76-1, edition 2006, accuracy classes II, III, IIII
- Date issued: 03.09.2013 (from signature dates)
- Page total: 4
- Test report: No. 1.12-4036945, Revision 2, and associated test reports No. 1.12-4036945/6, /7, /8 (all BD SI 200). Former test reports: No. 1.12-4036945/5 (Sample 1, DX SI 300) remains valid. Others have blank numbers.

Revision history: Revision 2 — the document is "Revision 2" but we don't have explicit revision history beyond that. Actually the certificate mentions transfer from old owner Sartorius AG to new owner Sartorius Industrial Scales GmbH & Co. KG. That's a transfer, might be part of revision history. Hmm. The revision is "Revision 2" and date 03.09.2013. I could record revision_history: [{revision: "2", date: "2013-09-03", changes: "Certificate transferred from Sartorius AG to Sartorius Industrial Scales GmbH & Co. KG"}]. That seems reasonable but slightly inferential. The page says "The above-mentioned OIML certificate is transferred from the old owner... to the new owner". So Revision 2 likely corresponds to this transfer. I'll include it.

Now the tables — these are the model matrices.

Table 1: BD SI 200, Class II
Two column variants (two configurations?):
- Variant A: Max 1 g ... 620 g; e 0.01 g ... 0.1 g; d 0.001 g ... 0.1 g; n ≤ 62000; Nominal capacity of load receptor 744 g; Initial zero setting + dead load ≤ 743 g
- Variant B: Max 500 g ... 6100 g; e 0.1 g ... 1 g; d 0.01 g ... 1 g; n ≤ 61000; Nominal capacity 7320 g; Initial zero setting + dead load ≤ 6820 g
Common: Tare-balancing range ≤ 100% of Max; Temperature range 10 °C / 30 °C

Wait — Max as range "1 g ... 620 g" — this is a multi-interval instrument? Actually for BD SI 200, Max ranges from 1 g to 620 g in variant A. This looks like the instrument can be configured with Max anywhere in 1–620 g. These are ranges of permissible Max/e configurations. Hmm, in German PTB certs for weighing instruments, "Max" given as a range means the maximum capacity can be set anywhere within the range. e also as a range. n ≤ 62000.

So the two columns are two variants of BD SI 200 — probably differing by load receptor / platform size. I'll treat them as model variants: "BD SI 200" with two sub-variants. How to name? Could label them "BD SI 200 (variant 1)" and "BD SI 200 (variant 2)". Or use the distinguishing Max ranges.

Similarly Table 2: BG SI 200, Class II, two variants:
- Variant A: Max 2.5–15 kg, e 0.5–2 g, d 0.5–2 g, n≤30000, Nominal capacity 21 kg, Initial zero setting+dead load ≤ 18.5 kg
- Variant B: Max 5–35 kg, e 1–5 g, d 0.1–5 g, n≤35000, Nominal capacity 41 kg, Initial zero+dead load ≤ 36 kg
Common: Tare ≤100% Max, Temperature 10°C/30°C

Table 3: DG SI 300, Class (III), four variants:
- V1: Max 0.1–6 kg, e 1–10 g, n≤6000, n_i≤3000, Nominal cap 7.8 kg, init zero 7.7 kg
- V2: Max 0.2–15 kg, e 2–20 g, n≤7500, n_i≤3000, Nominal cap 19.5 kg, init zero 19.3 kg
- V3: Max 2.5–35 kg, e 5–50 g, n≤7000, n_i≤3500, Nominal cap 44 kg, init zero 41.5 kg
- V4: Max 5–60 kg, e 10–100 g, n≤6000, n_i≤3000, Nominal cap 78 kg, init zero 73 kg
Common: Tare ≤100% Max, Temperature -10°C/+40°C
DG SI 300 is a multiple range instrument (n_i (Max_i/e_i) ≤).

Table 4: DX SI 300, two accuracy classes (III) and (IIII):
- (III): Max 0.5 kg ... 300 t; n≤6125, n_i≤3125, n_i≤3125 (multi-interval Max_i/e_i), n_1≤6250
- (IIII): Max 0.5 kg ... 300 t; n≤1000, n_i≤1000, n_i≤1000, n_1≤6250
Common: Tare-balancing 100% Max; Preset tare 100% Max (1) / 100% Max_1 (2); Temperature -10°C/+40°C
Footnotes: 1) applies to each range of single- and multiple range instruments; 2) applies only to multi-interval instruments.

Footnotes overall:
- 1) "The sum of Max, initial zero-setting range and the dead load shall not exceed the nominal capacity of the load receptor." (Tables 1-3)
- 1) "This applies to each range of single- and multiple range instruments" (Table 4)
- 2) "This applies only to multi-interval instruments" (Table 4)

The footnote markers repeat "1)" with different text per table. I'll list them all in footnotes array with the same marker but different texts — perhaps with a note about which table. The schema is footnotes[]: marker, text. I can list three entries: marker "1)" (tables 1-3), marker "1)" (table 4), marker "2)" (table 4). To disambiguate, I could add text including context. Maybe make text plain but I can append "(Table 4)" as context? That would alter the text. Better to keep the text verbatim; duplicates are acceptable.

Now let's design the model family. The cert covers 4 types with multiple variants. Total variants: BD SI 200 ×2, BG SI 200 ×2, DG SI 300 ×4, DX SI 300 ×2 (by class). 

Model family models: I'll create model_ids like:
- "BD SI 200 variant 1 (Max 1 g–620 g)" — hmm, simpler: "BD SI 200 (column 1)"? Better to be descriptive: use nominal capacities? Actually the distinguishing feature between the BD variants: variant 1 nominal capacity 744 g vs variant 2 7320 g. For BG: 21 kg vs 41 kg. For DG: 7.8, 19.5, 44, 78 kg. For DX: class III vs IIII.

I'll define models with model_id strings:
- "BD SI 200 / 744 g load receptor"
- "BD SI 200 / 7320 g load receptor"
- "BG SI 200 / 21 kg load receptor"
- "BG SI 200 / 41 kg load receptor"
- "DG SI 300 / 7.8 kg load receptor"
- "DG SI 300 / 19.5 kg load receptor"
- "DG SI 300 / 44 kg load receptor"
- "DG SI 300 / 78 kg load receptor"
- "DX SI 300 class III"
- "DX SI 300 class IIII"

Alternatively simpler ids: "BD SI 200 (1)", "BD SI 200 (2)", etc. I think using nominal capacity descriptors is more informative. Let me use e.g. "BD SI 200 [A]"? Hmm. I'll go with "BD SI 200 / max 1–620 g" style? The max is a range though. Nominal capacity of load receptor is a single number and distinguishes variants well. I'll use that.

Actually for DX SI 300, the two variants differ by accuracy class, so name by class.

model_level characteristics: I need attribute × model matrix. Attributes:

For BD SI 200:
- maximum_capacity (Max): value is a range {min,max}, unit g. Variant A: 1–620 g; variant B: 500–6100 g.
- scale_interval_e: range in g: 0.01–0.1; 0.1–1
- actual_scale_interval_d: 0.001–0.1; 0.01–1
- max_number_of_scale_intervals_n: 62000; 61000
- nominal_capacity_of_load_receptor: 744 g; 7320 g
- initial_zero_setting_plus_dead_load_max: 743 g; 6820 g

Type-level for BD: tare_balancing_range: ≤100% of Max; temperature_range: 10–30 °C; accuracy_class II.

But the schema has type_level as whole-cert attributes and model_level as matrix across models. Since different types have different temperature ranges, temperature becomes model-level too (grouped). I can create model_level entries with values per model, even if values repeat across models within a type.

Given complexity, maybe the cleanest approach: put per-model attributes in model_level arrays with entries for each of the 10 models, and matrix_tables for the raw tables.

Alternatively, treat each type as its own mini-family and emit matrix_tables for Tables 1–4 with rows as variants. The schema's matrix_tables allow arbitrary multi-dim tables. I'll do both: matrix_tables (4 tables) and model_level characteristics.

Let me define model_level entries (values across all 10 models):

1. maximum_capacity, unit g (mixed units: g and kg and t for DX — messy). Unit differs per model. Hmm. For DX: Max 0.5 kg ... 300 t — mixed units within one range! 0.5 kg to 300 t. Convert to kg: 0.5–300000 kg. Hmm, but original says "0.5 kg ... 300 t". I could record value {min: 0.5, max: 300000}, unit kg, but that changes original. Or keep value as string "0.5 kg ... 300 t". Rules say ranges become {min,max} numbers. I'll convert to kg: min 0.5, max 300000, unit "kg". Actually, maybe keep "t" as unit? No — min is in kg. Converting is the sane approach. But then DG BG BD also should be in a consistent unit. Let me convert all Max to kg for uniformity? BD: 1 g = 0.001 kg... That loses fidelity. Hmm.

Alternative: keep attribute-level unit g for BD and DG small? The schema's model_level entry has a single unit_symbol for all values. So per attribute I need one unit. I could split into separate attributes per type, e.g. maximum_capacity with unit per value? No — values[] entries have {model, value, footnote_markers} — no unit per value per the example. But I could create separate model_level entries per type:
- "maximum_capacity" with mixed units is bad.

Option: use unit "kg" for all and convert:
- BD A: 0.001–0.62 kg; BD B: 0.5–6.1 kg
- BG A: 2.5–15 kg; BG B: 5–35 kg
- DG: 0.1–6; 0.2–15; 2.5–35; 5–60 kg
- DX: 0.5–300000 kg

Similarly e and d:
- BD A: e 0.01–0.1 g → 0.00001–0.0001 kg. Ugly but consistent. Hmm.

Maybe better: keep units as given and emit separate model_level entries per attribute per unit context, e.g. attribute "maximum_capacity" can't have multiple unit entries... Actually I could emit multiple model_level entries with the same attribute but... no, that would collide.

Alternative approach: define attributes with units as in original tables, but split by type using attribute names? The schema allows attribute as free string. But duplicating attribute names with different units is confusing.

Perhaps simplest and most faithful: since each type forms its own group, and the schema also has matrix_tables where I can preserve exact original values, I can:
- Emit matrix_tables for Tables 1–4 with exact original text values (with ranges like "1 g ... 620 g" → {min, max, unit} per cell? The rows are objects with values; example shows numeric values). In the R137 example, rows have numeric values and column_units array gives the unit. So cells should be numbers and column_units give units. For our tables, Max is a range → value can be {min, max}. column_units: "g" etc. For DX "0.5 kg ... 300 t" mixed — I'd convert to kg for that column (300 t = 300000 kg) and note in description, or keep as string. In matrix tables rows I could use numbers; for DX I'll put {"min": 0.5, "max": 300000} with column_unit "kg" and add description noting original "0.5 kg ... 300 t".

- Emit model_level characteristics per attribute with a single unit. Given mixed units across types, I'll convert everything to kg for mass attributes (max, nominal capacity, initial zero setting) and to g for e and d? Hmm, e and d also span types. Let me think about which attributes to include in model_level.

Actually maybe cleaner: model_level attributes with per-type splitting isn't allowed... but I can include the unit in values? The schema example shows values[]: {model, value, footnote_markers[]}. Strictly no unit per value. So single unit per attribute.

Decision: convert all mass quantities to kg:
- maximum_capacity (kg): BD A 0.001–0.62; BD B 0.5–6.1; BG A 2.5–15; BG B 5–35; DG1 0.1–6; DG2 0.2–15; DG3 2.5–35; DG4 5–60; DX III 0.5–300000; DX IIII 0.5–300000.
- verification_scale_interval_e (kg): BD A 0.00001–0.0001; BD B 0.0001–0.001; BG A 0.0005–0.002; BG B 0.001–0.005; DG1 0.001–0.01; DG2 0.002–0.02; DG3 0.005–0.05; DG4 0.01–0.1; DX: not given in table (Max/e implied). DX e not listed; skip for DX.
- actual_scale_interval_d (kg): BD A 0.000001–0.0001; BD B 0.00001–0.001; BG A 0.0005–0.002; BG B 0.0001–0.005; DG/DX not given.

Hmm, these conversions get ugly. Alternative: keep g units for e/d: then DX missing — fine, just omit DX from values for that attribute. But the rule of single unit per attribute: e in g: BD A 0.01–0.1 g; BD B 0.1–1 g; BG A 0.5–2 g; BG B 1–5 g; DG1 1–10 g; DG2 2–20 g; DG3 5–50 g; DG4 10–100 g. That's clean in g. d in g: BD A 0.001–0.1; BD B 0.01–1; BG A 0.5–2; BG B 0.1–5. Clean.

Max in kg? BD A would be 0.001–0.62 kg. Or Max in g for BD (1–620), kg for BG/DG, t for DX... conflicting.

Alternative: keep max in kg as decided. It's fine — fidelity preserved in matrix_tables where I can keep original. Actually wait — in matrix_tables, cells for Max for BD: {min: 1, max: 620} with column unit "g". For DX: {min: 0.5, max: 300000}? original "0.5 kg ... 300 t". Hmm, or keep DX cell as string "0.5 kg ... 300 t". The example shows numeric cells but strings are allowed in JSON. I think converting is cleaner: value {min: 0.5, max: 300000}, unit kg, and description mentions original.

Hmm wait, actually maybe I should reconsider: perhaps treat "Max 0.5 kg ... 300 t" as the capability range of the instrument family — the smallest Max is 0.5 kg and largest 300 t. Converting to kg: 0.5 to 300000. Good.

- max_number_of_scale_intervals (dimensionless): BD A 62000; BD B 61000; BG A 30000; BG B 35000; DG1 6000; DG2 7500; DG3 7000; DG4 6000; DX III 6125; DX IIII 1000. Attribute "max_number_of_verification_scale_intervals_n".
- accuracy_class: BD models "II"; BG "II"; DG "III"; DX III "III"; DX IIII "IIII". Attribute "accuracy_class" values strings.
- nominal_capacity_of_load_receptor (kg): BD A 0.744; BD B 7.32; BG A 21; BG B 41; DG 7.8/19.5/44/78; DX not given. Hmm conversions: 744 g = 0.744 kg; 7320 g = 7.32 kg.
- initial_zero_setting_plus_dead_load_maximum (kg): 0.743; 6.82; 18.5; 36; 7.7; 19.3; 41.5; 73; DX not given. footnote marker 1) for these (tables 1–3 footnote).
- DG multiple range instrument n_i ≤: 3000, 3000, 3500, 3000 (only DG). Attribute "multiple_range_instrument_ni_max" values for DG models only. I can include only DG models in values[] — omit others (don't fabricate).
- DX attributes: n for single range (6125 / 1000), n_i for multiple range (3125 / 1000), n_i multi-interval (3125 / 1000), n_1 multi-interval (6250 / 6250). These are DX-specific. Attributes: "single_range_instrument_max_over_e_n_max", "multiple_range_instrument_maxi_over_ei_ni_max", "multi_interval_instrument_maxi_over_ei_ni_max", "multi_interval_instrument_maxi_over_e1_n1_max". For DX models only.
- tare_balancing_range: "100% of Max" — value 100, unit %, reference Max. Type-level? It's same across all models: "100 % of Max". Could be type_level with value 100 unit "%" and reference note. Hmm, the strict value object: {"value": 100, "unit_symbol": "%"} plus maybe a separate string? I'll add attribute tare_balancing_range as type_level: {value: 100, unit_symbol: "%", footnote_markers: []} and maybe tare_reference "Max". Actually simpler: value string "100 % of Max"? Rules say numbers not strings for numeric. "100% of Max" is a percentage-of-reference expression. I'll do: type_level "tare_balancing_range": {value: 100, unit_symbol: "%", footnote_markers: []} and maybe separate "tare_balancing_range_reference": {value: "Max"}. For DX preset tare with footnotes 1 and 2 — preset tare range 100% of Max (marker 1), 100% of Max_1 (marker 2). That's DX-specific: model_level or config? It varies by instrument range type (single/multiple vs multi-interval) — that's a configuration axis. Could put in config_level: attribute "preset_tare_range", axis "instrument_range_type", conditions "single- and multiple range instruments" → 100% of Max marker 1; "multi-interval instruments" → 100% of Max_1 marker 2. 

- temperature_range: BD/BG: 10–30 °C; DG/DX: -10–+40 °C. Model-level: values per model {min,max} unit °C. Or config-level by type. Model_level is fine: values for 10 models.

Type-level (whole-cert):
- tare_balancing_range: 100 % of Max (applies to all).
- Hmm actually temperature differs by type, so model_level.

Let me also consider accuracy_class at model_level as noted.

Also "module_designation": for R76 weighing instruments, module concept... The certified type is a complete instrument — "Nonautomatic electromechanical weighing instrument with or without lever system". Module designation: Not applicable? The schema says module_designation: "Analog load cell" | "Not applicable" | null. For a complete weighing instrument certificate, I'd say null or "Not applicable". Hmm, R76 certs often cover complete instruments. I'll put null (omit? schema shows field). I'll set "Not applicable"? Risky fabrication. I'll omit or null. The schema lists it with those examples; for completeness I'll use null.

category: "Nonautomatic weighing instrument" — schema examples: "Load cell", "Indicator", ... For R76, "Weighing instrument" fits. I'll use "Nonautomatic weighing instrument".

type_designations: ["BD SI 200", "BG SI 200", "DG SI 300", "DX SI 300"].

description: "Nonautomatic electromechanical weighing instrument with or without lever system".

recommendation: id "R76", edition 2006, amendment — the cert says "R76-1, edition 2006". Part 1. Canonical id "R76", edition 2006. Maybe note part? Schema has no part field. I could set id "R76" and edition 2006. Or id "R76-1"? The rule example: canonical e.g. "R60" not "OIML R 60". For R76-1, canonical might be "R76-1"? Hmm. I think "R76" with edition 2006; but the "-1" part is meaningful (R76-1 covers metrological requirements). I'll use "R76-1"? The rule says canonical like "R60". R76-1 is how OIML designates it. I'll go with "R76-1" since it's the actual recommendation designation. Hmm, but example "R60" not "OIML R 60" — about stripping "OIML". I'll use "R76-1". Actually let me reconsider: the schema example says id (canonical, e.g. "R60" not "OIML R 60"). For a part-numbered recommendation, the canonical id includes the part: "R76-1". I'll use "R76-1".

accuracy_classes: ["II", "III", "IIII"] (as (II) (III) (IIII)).

scheme: The certificate number R76/2006-DE1-08.03 — scheme is A or B per schema (certificate.scheme). OIML-CS scheme A = certificate including type evaluation report review; scheme B = without. Can't determine from doc; omit or null. I'll omit.
